lesson.menu_title: Precision Under Pressure -- Fluency Drilling and Register Control in High-Stakes Tax Advisory Calls
lesson.menu_desc: No new grammar: reported speech, gerunds and infinitives and the passive, all at once, in a four-sentence turn that survives an adversarial client call -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 11 -- Precision Under Pressure
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Leonardo Constantino | Lesson 11 -- Fluency and Register Control
lesson.grammar_point: fluency and register control -- integrated production of reported speech, gerunds and infinitives and the passive (no new form)

listenings.text: Leonardo, it is Priya Raghavan, general counsel at Northgate. I am calling before Thursday because I would rather you heard this from me than from Dana in front of her board. Three things. First, our auditors sent a note last night saying the whole structure would be challenged. I do not agree with them, but Dana has read it twice and she has underlined it. Second, and I am sorry to say this, the word limited in your last memo has become a problem. She read it as the amount. Your team meant the scope. Nobody explained the difference, and now it looks as if somebody was softening bad news on purpose. Third. Dana does not want you to agree with her. She wants you to hold a position and say why. The last adviser who sat in that chair agreed with everything she said, and she stopped calling him in April. So concede what is genuinely arguable, push back on the rest, and please, whatever you do, do not tell her that everything will be fine. She will not believe you, and she will be right.

I want to tell you about the most expensive habit I see in advisers who work in a second language. It is not grammar. It is the retreat. Somebody asks a hard question, the adviser answers in one short sentence, and then stops. The room reads that silence as doubt. Then, to fill it, the adviser starts hedging. Maybe. Possibly. It could be. In some cases. And by the fourth qualifier nobody in that room believes there is a view at all. Here is the thing about hedging. A hedge is a tool, and like every tool it has a size. One hedge protects you. Four hedges tell everyone you are afraid of the question. And the cure is not to hedge less. The cure is to hold the floor for four sentences instead of one. Say what you think. Say the one thing that is genuinely uncertain, and say why it is uncertain. Concede the point they are right about, because conceding a small point is what buys you the big one. Then say what you would do. That is four sentences, it works in any language, and it only works if you stay in the room long enough to finish it. Most people lose the argument in the pause after the first sentence.

extra_audio.text: I take the point, and I concede that the timing is aggressive. But the exposure is not zero, and I should clarify what the note meant. To be more precise, only the intercompany fees are exposed. Let me back up that claim with the treaty text before you decide. What we are recommending is a smaller change, not a full restructuring.
